questions.prompt: What keeps a planet orbiting the Sun instead of flying off into space?
options: The Sun's light pushes the planet along
Gravity pulls it inward while its own forward motion carries it past, and the two balance into a loop
Invisible rails guide each planet
The planets are magnetically stuck to the Sun
questions.explanation: A planet keeps going forward on its own; the Sun's gravity constantly bends that motion inward. Together, forward motion and inward pull trace a closed loop — the orbit.
questions.misconception: It is natural to imagine an orbit as a rail or a magnetic stick, but neither exists: gravity keeps bending the planet's path inward, and the orbit is really an endless fall that keeps missing the Sun.

questions.prompt: Why does Neptune's orbit take so much longer than Mercury's?
options: Neptune is heavier and therefore moves faster
Distance sets both the size of the path and the speed along it: Neptune's loop is many times wider and Neptune drifts along it more slowly
The Sun's gravity only reaches the inner planets
Neptune stops and restarts during its year
questions.explanation: Being farther out gives a planet two penalties at once: a much longer path to travel, and a slower speed along it. Together they stretch Neptune's year to about 165 Earth years against Mercury's 88 days.
questions.misconception: Some learners think only the longer path matters, or that the Sun 'pulls harder' on nearby planets. In fact extra distance both widens the loop and slows the drift — the two combine into the enormous year.

questions.prompt: What shape do planet orbits follow?
options: Perfect circles with the Sun at the exact center
Ellipses with the Sun at one focus
Figure-eights looping around the Sun
Spirals that slowly wind outward
questions.explanation: Each planet follows an ellipse — a slightly squashed circle — with the Sun at one of its two focus points, which is why a planet's distance from the Sun changes a little during its year.
questions.misconception: Most diagrams show perfect circles, but real orbits are ellipses. For planets the squash is tiny; for comets it is huge, and their stretched ellipses dive in close to the Sun then swing far out.

Between Earth and Mars
Beyond Neptune
Just inside Mercury's orbit
questions.explanation: The asteroid belt orbits in the wide gap between Mars (1.5 AU) and Jupiter (5.2 AU) — the solar system's largest orbital gap — made of rocky leftovers that never joined to form a planet.
questions.misconception: The Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune holds icy worlds like Pluto; confusing the asteroid belt (rocky, Mars–Jupiter gap) with the Kuiper Belt (icy, beyond Neptune) is a common mix-up.

questions.prompt: If the Sun's gravity suddenly switched off, what would Earth do?
options: Stop in place
Fly off in a straight line in whatever direction it was moving at that moment
Orbit faster
Spiral down into where the Sun used to be
questions.explanation: With no inward pull, nothing bends Earth's motion anymore — it would continue in a straight line along the direction it was heading when the force vanished.
questions.misconception: It feels right that 'gravity stops' should make a planet fall in — but falling in was never the planet's natural state. Straight-line motion is; gravity is what bends that straight line into a loop.
